headline: Halfway Rock on the ebb: mackerel thick, bass tightening toward the river mouths
subhead: The new moon tide finally moved bait and bass together, and Casco Bay's ledges are showing the first real fall signals of the season.
body_markdown:
Stand on the seawall at Two Lights on a falling tide this week and the story writes itself in the birds. Terns and gulls are working tight little knots over the outer flats, diving on bait that's been pushed shoreward by the biggest tidal swing of early fall. That's the September 10th new moon doing its work — the strongest push we've seen since August — and it's squeezing peanut bunker and mackerel against the beaches, the river mouths, and the granite edges of the outer islands. We flagged this pattern building back on September 7th, noting that bait concentrations would tighten as we moved toward mid-month, and that's exactly the shape the bay has taken this week.

Water's cooling into that transitional range where September fishing in Casco Bay always gets interesting — not summer-warm, not fall-cold, but sliding through the window where mackerel schools thicken up, bass start staging for their coastal exit, and the first cod and haddock interest of the season starts showing on the deeper ledges. The bay hasn't flipped over yet, but the signs are there for anyone paying attention to bottom structure and tide stage.

Halfway Rock remains the anchor point for this zone, and it's fishing the way it always does this time of year — better on the last two hours of the ebb and first hour of the new flood, when the current sets up along the eastern face of the ledge and pushes bait past the rock in a predictable seam. Bass in the 24 to 32 inch range have been coming off that structure on live mackerel fished on a fish-finder rig, 20 to 40 feet down where the ledge drops into deeper water on the northeast corner. A few boats working topwater poppers and Deceiver-style flies at first light have connected too, though that bite has been more sunrise-dependent than tide-dependent — worth being on the water by 5:30, not 7.

Mackerel themselves have been the story of the week more than the bass. Schools are thick around Peaks Island, particularly off the eastern side toward Diamond Cove, and along the drop-off north of Bailey Island where the bottom falls from 20 feet to better than 60 inside a quarter mile. Small chrome Norwegian-style jigs, size 1 to 2, fished on a three-hook mackerel tree, have been filling coolers fast enough that some boats are catching their bait limit in twenty minutes and moving on to bass and bluefish. That's the value of a strong mackerel week — it's not just a fishery in its own right, it's bait for everything else swimming behind it.

Bluefish have shown in patches around Cape Small and the outer reaches of Harpswell, mostly smaller fish in the 2 to 4 pound class, but there have been a few reports of better fish — 6 to 8 pounds — busting mackerel schools on the surface off Cape Small's outer ledges on the last of the ebb. Diamond jigs worked fast on the retrieit, or simply cast metal like a Hopkins or a Kastmaster into the surface commotion, have been enough. No wire leader necessary at that size, but a short piece of 40-pound fluorocarbon will save some lures.

Striped bass overall are doing what we expected — committing harder to bait than they have all summer, staging near the mouths of the Presumpscot and the Royal River as bunker schools tighten under this moon's influence. That's the classic early fall pattern for this bay: fish stop picking at stragglers and start working bait in earnest, which is a meaningfully different bite than what anglers were dealing with in August. The best window has consistently been the two hours around the top of the tide near river mouths, when bass push up into the current to ambush bait getting funneled out. Live mackerel or bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, or a white bucktail with a chunk of pork rind trailer bounced along bottom, have both worked.

Groundfish interest is starting to stir but hasn't turned into a real fishery yet. A few boats working the deeper ledges off Halfway Rock and out toward the mouth of the bay have picked at cod and a scattering of haddock in 80 to 120 feet, mostly on diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid or clam. It's early — this bite typically doesn't get serious until the water drops another five degrees or so — but the interest is there, and it's worth noting because that's usually the first sign the bay is turning toward its late-fall groundfish pattern.

Looking ahead, the tide is still carrying residual push from the new moon, and that should keep bait tight and predators committed through the weekend. If the wind stays out of the northwest and holds under 15 knots, the outer ledges — Halfway Rock, the eastern drop at Peaks, the Cape Small structure — should keep producing on the ebb-to-flood transition. If a southerly wind develops and pushes swell into the bay, shift inside to Harpswell's protected coves and the river mouths, where bass will still be working bait regardless of sea state outside. The bigger picture: this week likely marks the start of the real fall progression, not the peak of it. Expect bait to keep tightening, bass to keep committing harder, and groundfish interest to build steadily as the water continues its seasonal slide.
